{{Short description|none}}
{{refimprove|date=March 2010}}
[[Clinical trial]]s are [[clinical research|medical research studies]] conducted on human subjects.<ref name="mlp">{{cite web |title=Clinical trials |url=https://medlineplus.gov/clinicaltrials.html |publisher=MedlinePlus, US National Library of Medicine |access-date=28 June 2022 |date=18 May 2018}}</ref> The human subjects are assigned to one or more interventions, and the investigators evaluate the effects of those interventions.<ref name=mlp/><ref>{{Cite web |title=NIH's Definition of a Clinical Trial {{!}} grants.nih.gov |url=https://grants.nih.gov/policy-and-compliance/policy-topics/clinical-trials/definition |access-date=2022-06-27 |website=grants.nih.gov}}</ref> The progress and results of clinical trials are analyzed statistically.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Amrhein |first1=Valentin |last2=Greenland |first2=Sander |last3=McShane |first3=Blakeley B. |date=1 December 2019 |title=Statistical significance gives bias a free pass |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/eci.13176 |journal=European Journal of Clinical Investigation |language=en |volume=49 |issue=12 |article-number=e13176 |doi=10.1111/eci.13176 |pmid=31610012 |s2cid=204702258 |issn=0014-2972|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/24450 |title=Critical Thinking in Clinical Research: Applied Theory and Practice Using Case Studies |year=2018 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-027280-7 |language=en-US |doi=10.1093/med/9780199324491.001.0001 |editor-last1=Fregni |editor-last2=Illigens |editor-first1=Felipe |editor-first2=Ben M.W. }}</ref>

==Analysis factors ==

=== Intention to treat ===
{{main|Intention to treat analysis}}
[[Randomized controlled trial|Randomized clinical trials]] analyzed by the [[intention to treat analysis|intention-to-treat]] (ITT) approach provide fair comparisons among the treatment groups because it avoids the [[bias (statistics)|bias]] associated with the non-random loss of the participants.<ref name="mon">{{cite journal | last1=Montori | first1=Victor M. | last2=Guyatt | first2=Gordon H. | title=Intention-to-treat principle | journal=Canadian Medical Association Journal | volume=165 | issue=10 | date=2001-11-11 | pages=1339–1341 | pmid=11760981 | pmc=81628}}</ref><ref name="als">{{Cite journal | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0049163| pmid=23166608| pmc=3499557|display-authors=3|title = Inconsistent Definitions for Intention-To-Treat in Relation to Missing Outcome Data: Systematic Review of the Methods Literature| journal=PLOS ONE| volume=7| issue=11| article-number=e49163|year = 2012|last1 = Alshurafa|first1 = Mohamad| last2=Briel| first2=Matthias| last3=Akl| first3=Elie A.| last4=Haines| first4=Ted| last5=Moayyedi| first5=Paul| last6=Gentles| first6=Stephen J.| last7=Rios| first7=Lorena| last8=Tran| first8=Chau| last9=Bhatnagar| first9=Neera| last10=Lamontagne| first10=Francois| last11=Walter| first11=Stephen D.| last12=Guyatt| first12=Gordon H.| bibcode=2012PLoSO...749163A| doi-access=free}}</ref> The basic ITT principle is that participants in the trials should be analysed in the groups to which they were randomized, regardless of whether they received or [[compliance (medicine)|adhered]] to the allocated intervention.<ref name=mon/> However, medical investigators often have difficulties in accepting ITT analysis because of clinical trial issues like missing data or adherence to [[clinical trial protocol|protocol]].<ref name=als/>

=== Per protocol ===
This analysis can be restricted to only the participants who fulfill the protocol in terms of the eligibility, adherence to the intervention, and outcome assessment. This analysis is known as an "on-treatment" or "per protocol" analysis. A per-protocol analysis represents a "best-case scenario" to reveal the effect of the drug being studied. However, by restricting the analysis to a selected patient population, it does not show all effects of the new drug. Further, adherence to treatment may be affected by other factors that influence the outcome. Accordingly, per-protocol effects are at risk of bias, whereas the intent-to-treat estimate is not.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sussman|first1=Jeremy B.|last2=Hayward|first2=Rodney A.|date=2010-05-04|title=An IV for the RCT: using instrumental variables to adjust for treatment contamination in randomised controlled trials|journal=BMJ (Clinical Research Ed.)|volume=340|article-number=c2073|doi=10.1136/bmj.c2073|issn=1756-1833|pmc=3230230|pmid=20442226}}</ref>

== Handling missing data ==
{{main|Missing data}}

=== Last observation carried forward ===
One method of handling missing data is simply to [[imputation (statistics)|impute]], or fill in, values based on existing data. A standard method to do this is the Last-Observation-Carried-Forward (LOCF) method.

The LOCF method allows for the analysis of the data. However, recent research shows that this method gives a biased estimate of the treatment effect and [[underestimated|underestimates]] the variability of the estimated result.<ref name="salim">{{Cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.psychres.2007.08.005| pmid=18718673|title = Comparison of data analysis strategies for intent-to-treat analysis in pre-test–post-test designs with substantial dropout rates| journal=Psychiatry Research| volume=160| issue=3| pages=335–345|year = 2008|last1 = Salim|first1 = Agus| last2=MacKinnon| first2=Andrew| last3=Christensen| first3=Helen| last4=Griffiths| first4=Kathleen| s2cid=23997894}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi=10.1503/cmaj.080820| pmid=18838445| pmc=2553855|title = Does analysis using "last observation carried forward" introduce bias in dementia research?| journal=Canadian Medical Association Journal| volume=179| issue=8| pages=751–753|year = 2008|last1 = Molnar|first1 = F. J.| last2=Hutton| first2=B.| last3=Fergusson| first3=D.}}</ref> As an example, assume that there are 8 weekly assessments after the baseline observation. If a patient drops out of the study after the third week, then this value is "carried forward" and assumed to be his or her score for the 5 missing data points. The assumption is that the patients improve gradually from the start of the study until the end, so that carrying forward an intermediate value is a conservative estimate of how well the person would have done had he or she remained in the study. The advantages to the LOCF approach are that: 
* It minimises the number of the subjects who are eliminated from the analysis, and
* It allows the analysis to examine the trends over time, rather than focusing simply on the endpoint.

However, the [[National Academy of Sciences]], in an advisory report to the [[Food and Drug Administration]] on missing data in clinical trials, recommended against the uncritical use of methods like LOCF, stating that "Single imputation methods like last observation carried forward and baseline observation carried forward should not be used as the primary approach to the treatment of missing data unless the assumptions that underlie them are scientifically justified."<ref name="trials">{{Cite book |url=http://www.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=12955 |pages=110–112 |doi=10.17226/12955|pmid=24983040 |pmc=3771340 |title=The Prevention and Treatment of Missing Data in Clinical Trials |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-309-15814-5 |author=National Research Council|author2=Division of Behavioral and Social Sciences and Education|author3=Committee on National Statistics|author4=Panel on Handling Missing Data in Clinical Trials|hdl=1942/14310 }}</ref>

=== Multiple imputation methods ===
{{main|Multiple imputation}}
The National Academy of Sciences advisory panel instead recommended methods that provide valid [[type I error]] rates under explicitly stated assumptions taking missing data status into account, and the use of multiple imputation methods based on all the data available in the model. It recommended more widespread use of [[Bootstrapping (statistics)|Bootstrap]] and [[Generalized estimating equation]] methods whenever the assumptions underlying them, such as [[Missing data|Missing at Random]] for [[Generalized estimating equation|GEE]] methods, can be justified. It advised collecting auxiliary data believed to be associated with dropouts to provide more robust and reliable models, collecting information about reason for drop-out; and, if possible, following up on drop-outs and obtaining efficacy outcome data. Finally, it recommended sensitivity analyses as part of clinical trial reporting to assess the [[Sensitivity analysis|sensitivity]] of the results to the assumptions about the missing data mechanism.<ref name="trials" />

While the methods recommended by the National Academy of Science report are more recently developed, more [[Robust statistics|robust]], and will work under a wider variety of conditions than single-imputation methods like LOCF, no known method for handling missing data is valid under all conditions. As the 1998 [[International Conference on Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Registration of Pharmaceuticals for Human Use|International Conference on Harmonization]] E9 Guidance on Statisticial Principles for Clinical Trials noted, "Unfortunately, no universally applicable methods of handling missing values can be recommended."<ref name="fda.gov">[https://web.archive.org/web/20090710000858/http://www.fda.gov/downloads/Drugs/GuidanceComplianceRegulatoryInformation/Guidances/ucm073137.pdf International Conference on Harmonization, Guidance for Industry E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials], 1998</ref> Expert statistical and medical judgment must select the method most appropriate to the particularly trial conditions of the available imperfect techniques, depending on the particular trial's goals, endpoints, statistical methods, and context.

== Estimands ==
To promote better consistency between a trial's objective and analysis methods, addendum to the ICH E9 guidance on statistical principles for clinical trials (ICH E9(R1)) describes a framework for using estimands; an [[estimand]] is a clear description of the treatment effect a trial aims to quantify. <ref>{{cite web |title=ICH E9 (R1) addendum on estimands and sensitivity analysis in clinical trials to the guideline on statistical principles for clinical trials |url=https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/ich-e9-r1-addendum-estimands-and-sensitivity-analysis-clinical-trials-guideline-statistical-principles-clinical-trials-step-5_en.pdf}}</ref>  According to the ICH E9(R1) addendum, defining an estimand involves detailing the following five attributes: (i) population of patients; (ii) treatment conditions; (iii) the endpoint; (iv) the summary measure; and (v) how intercurrent events are handle.

There has been a growing recognition in literature that different analysis methods can be used to target different estimands.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pham |first1=Tra My |last2=Kahan |first2=Brennan |last3=Lopes |first3=Andre |last4=Rashid |first4=Memuna |last5=Hoskin |first5=Peter |last6=White |first6=Ian |title=Estimating treatment effects in trials with outcome data truncated by death: A case study on aligning estimators with estimands |journal=Clinical Trials |date=4 Oct 2025 |volume=22 |issue=6 |doi=10.1177/17407745251360645 |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/17407745251360645}}</ref> It is therefore important to consider analysis methods that target the chosen estimand and assess if these methods have the most realistic assumptions given the trial’s setting. A tutorial paper on how to implement the estimand framework is available.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kahan |first1=Brennan |last2=Hindley |first2=Joanna |last3=Edwards |first3=Mark |last4=Cro |first4=Suzie |last5=Morris |first5=Tim |title=The estimands framework: a primer on the ICH E9(R1) addendum |journal=BMJ |date=23 January 2024 |volume=384 |article-number=e076316 |doi=10.1136/bmj-2023-076316 |pmid=38262663 |pmc=10802140 |url=https://www.bmj.com/content/384/bmj-2023-076316}}</ref>
